decisions.decision: Open decisions are ranked across the 13 functions in one short queue. Each decision is owned by one function: its class's owner (the owning role's template function in decision rights, else the one function whose matrix lists the class), else the function of the record type it decides, else of a record it changes, else the venture. Its cross-function score is the decision index's score times its function's weight in the venture's phase over the mean weight, times 1.5 when it bears on a telos measure exactly one lead plan binds; ties break by score, then id. Decisions that change the same record or that one handoff executes form one theme, and the queue shows the top ten themes, one item each, with the function's lead. The rules are pure functions and the reading is in Effect (EE-125).
decisions.why: The person needs one short queue of what to decide next across all functions, weighted for the phase the venture is in (EE-126 phase weights) and for the measures leads are accountable for, without seeing the same question once per decision that touches it.

decisions.decision: The Lean Canvas (Maurya, Running Lean, 2012) is the venture's shared kernel in the sense of Evans' Domain-Driven Design: one page every function reads. Its nine boxes are references to record attributes, never copies, and each box is owned by the function the data model gives its record type; the strategy function owns the canvas itself, which only assembles and orders the boxes. Each box is fetchable at its own route (identity/lean-canvas/<box>) and shows what filling it unlocks: the phase gate that asks for its record, the function workflows that read it and the record types that reference it. The canvas is presented as a roadmap, the current phase's gate evidence first in the gate's order, so the founder sees the template and what each record unlocks instead of one-off questions. The decision queue raises a decision that settles a record the phase's gate asks for by 2 and breaks ties in the gate's order. venture.json core gains unfair_advantage.
decisions.why: Torian, 2026-11-22: rather than asking one-off questions, present the standard template for the records and the roadmap of what each one unlocks; the canvas is a nested component whose parts span functions and can be fetched from it, acting as a kernel of the venture. The queue had put the problem statement eighth in discovery although the gate asks for it first.

decisions.decision: Each phase gate item gets an evidence ladder and a policy, the way a password meter rates strength. The ladder is the evidence levels adapted from GRADE (very low, low, moderate, high), measured per item by counted evidence, the grade of the record's cited evidence, the plan's coverage of open items, or a person's act. Interviews are the strongest common proof but not the only one: desk research from three distinct sources reaches moderate, and behavior evidence from the target audience with five or more cases reaches high. A policy gives each item a minimum level and a boundary: fail-closed refuses the phase change when the item falls short, fail-open lets it pass and names the shortfall as an open risk. packages/naive/src/phases/gate-policies.json holds the eight discovery items (customer, problem, alternatives, solution-fit, channel, economic-signal, validation-plan, decision) and three presets, lenient, standard and strict, ranked by a strictness score from 0 to 100 (each item's minimum level index over 3, weighted 1 fail-closed and 0.25 fail-open, averaged). A venture picks a preset and may tune items under phase_gates in naive.config.json. The gate is report-only by default; it refuses a phase change only when phase_gates.enforce is true, and then only for fail-closed items. The decision item is satisfied by a person's phase change and never by an agent. The validation plan (validation/plan.json) names each open assumption with its test, passing result and date. Every threshold is an unvalidated prior, ours.
decisions.why: A gate that only asks whether records exist lets a venture leave discovery on a guess, and a gate that demands ten interviews for every item stops a founder whose best proof is behavior or desk research. Grading each item's evidence on one ladder and letting the venture choose how strict to be, with enforcement opted in, shows the founder how strong the case is without blocking work by default.

decisions.decision: Naive gets the Venture Anatomy Matrix, a sibling of the Product Anatomy Matrix, as the venture's architecture description in the sense of ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 (iso-42010-2022-architecture-description). The matrix is the root; each of its eleven sub-matrices (identity, customer, market, industry, product, competition, business model, team, capital, risk, traction) is a model held by record types the data model already has, owned by the function the data model gives its record type, and the strategy function owns the matrix itself, which copies nothing. Views come from viewpoints: the Lean Canvas is a view over the matrix, not a separate record, beside the Business Model Canvas (osterwalder-2004-business-model-ontology) and an S-1 outline (sec-form-s-1). Regulation S-K is the coverage check (sec-regulation-s-k, sec-2020-s-k-modernization): items 101 business, 105 risk factors, 303 MD&A, 401 management and 403 ownership, and the Regulation S-X financial statements, each map to at least one sub-matrix. Two new record types, market-anatomy (markets/<id>.json, marketing and sales) and industry-anatomy (industries/<id>.json, strategy), hold cells of one shared shape whose status is known, estimated or unknown; unknown is a value, never null, and every new venture starts with markets/primary.json and industries/primary.json with every cell unknown. Time travel is bitemporal (sql-2011-temporal): application time on each cell (valid_from, valid_to) and system time from the provenance log and the blob store (readAsOf). Thresholds for phase gates come from a calibration over the market and industry sub-matrices, which proposes a decision a person accepts and never sets a gate on its own. The thresholds are unvalidated priors, ours. Matrices live in Naive now, one per venture; industry matrices shared across ventures belong to Mentura later.
decisions.why: Torian, 2026-11-22: the venture needs one model that spans its functions and can be read at any time, so that what counts as enough evidence at a gate is derived from the venture's market and industry rather than fixed. Business architecture standards were compared (bizbok-15-business-architecture, gartner-2017-digital-twin-organization): ISO 42010 is the formal standard for an architecture description with views and viewpoints, the canvases are too narrow to be the whole model, and the disclosure items an S-1 requires are the most complete public list of what an investor asks about a company.

decisions.decision: Node 22.19 or later is the floor for Naive and for every venture. The root package.json and create-venture declare engines.node >=22.19.0, create-venture writes the same floor into each new venture's package.json, and CI runs on Node 22.19. This amends EE-087's sentence that ventures need no newer Node: ventures still need no TypeScript, but they need Node 22.19, because Effect is a runtime dependency (EE-125) and Effect 4 requires Node 22.19.

decisions.decision: Naive compiles on publish. The package ships dist/, a mirror of the files it ships at the same relative paths, in which every .ts and .mjs outside fixtures/ is compiled by tsc (.ts to .js, .mjs stays .mjs, relative .ts imports and string paths to compiled .ts files renamed to .js) and every other file is copied, so a module still finds its JSON, templates and scripts by its place in the tree. The package's exports and bin point into dist/, with a naive-framework/src/<file>.ts subpath resolving to the compiled .js; each code export's types condition names the source file, which the package still ships, so Naive emits no .d.ts files. npm runs the build (scripts/build.ts) as prepare, so a git dependency builds on install. Inside the repository, tests and CLIs run the source under Node's type stripping, and an installed create-venture runs the compiled copy. This is EE-087's fourth phase, done before the renaming instead of after it, and it amends EE-087's .d.ts files to a types condition. With it, the exception that modules an app or a venture reaches from node_modules stay .mjs ends: every new file is .ts.
decisions.why: Torian, 2026-11-22, agreeing to the TypeScript and Effect runtime plan (docs/design/TYPESCRIPT_AND_EFFECT_RUNTIME_2026-11-22.md, "The fix: compile on publish"): Node does not strip types under node_modules, so every module a venture reached from an installed copy had to stay JavaScript, and new work kept adding .mjs files. A mirror of the shipped tree was chosen over emitting next to the sources, because tsc cannot emit an .mjs input over itself and .mjs files that import .ts would stay broken.

decisions.decision: Every compiled file in dist/ is .mjs: a .ts module compiles to .mjs, not .js, and its imports and string paths are renamed to match, so a module converted from .mjs to .ts keeps the path apps and scripts already use (naive-framework/src/<file>.mjs and node <path>.mjs both keep working), and a naive-framework/src/<file>.ts subpath resolves to the same .mjs file. naiveScript finds a converted module by either name. This amends EE-159's .ts to .js. scripts/to-ts.ts converts modules by name: it renames each with git mv and rewrites every reference in the repository, so the rest of the migration runs unit by unit without breaking imports.
decisions.why: Torian, 2026-11-22: continue the TypeScript migration with a swarm. With .js output, every rename of an .mjs module an app imports (everything-ecosystem imports router.ts, provenance.ts, contract.ts and others by name) would break that app, and a re-export shim would break scripts that check whether they are the main module and could load one module twice.

decisions.decision: A venture runs its Effects through one runtime. ventureRuntime(dir, overrides) in packages/naive/src/core/effect/runtime.ts is a ManagedRuntime built from VentureLayer(dir, overrides), the layer of the venture's services: built on its first run, shared by every run after, and released by dispose, after which a run dies. The layer starts with VentureFs alone, NodeFs unless overrides.fs gives another layer (MemoryFs in a test); each other service in docs/design/TYPESCRIPT_AND_EFFECT_RUNTIME_2026-11-22.md joins it in its own phase, and those that read the venture's files read under dir. runSync, runPromise and runMain run through one such runtime for the process, so older callers keep their shapes. This is phase 2 of that design.
decisions.why: Built in the 2026-11-22 TypeScript migration swarm as the design's phase 2. One layer is the one place a venture's services are chosen, so a test or a host replaces a service by passing a layer, and later services join without changing the code that boots a runtime. A runtime per venture keeps two ventures' services and lifetimes apart, and the runners stop building NodeFs again on every run.

decisions.decision: Mentura is the official console for Naive, and Naive ships its own CLI. naive is the one command a founder needs: naive new starts a venture through create-venture, and any command naive does not have itself runs as the same mentura command, so routes, drafts, decisions and freshness run through naive inside a venture. mentura stays as an alias. Naive gets no console of its own. A paid tier of the CLI is planned (not built): capabilities open by license, checked through a hook the paid build registers, so Naive names no vendor.
decisions.why: Torian chose it on 2026-11-24 (decision card: Which console should Naive have?) after asking that Naive run completely from a CLI and that people may pay for the CLI. Naive is the engine and Mentura is hosted Naive (EE-041, EE-118), so one console is built once. A single command removes the split between naive and mentura that a new founder could not guess.

decisions.decision: Naive keeps the tools a business needs as data, in packages/naive/src/functions/tools.json: a three-level taxonomy of function (APQC level 1, departments.json), process group (APQC level 2, 72 groups) and tool. Each tool names its function, or none for the universal tools every business gets (home, decisions, agents, files, records, tasks, people, calendar, activity, connections, settings), the process groups it serves, the record types it reads and writes, and the record types it proposes where the data model has none yet. Consoles build their navigation from this file instead of a hand-kept list. A tool's status is derived from what it touches, never written. check-tools.ts holds every function and process group to at least one tool.
decisions.why: Torian asked on 2026-11-24 for the console to offer the tools a business needs across all of its functions and sub-functions, plus the universal tools, from an enumerated ontology rather than an ad hoc menu. APQC's Process Classification Framework already gives Naive its functions (EE-047), so its level 2 groups are the sub-functions, and tying each tool to record types keeps the console and the data model from drifting.

decisions.decision: Naive keeps the activities a business performs as data, in packages/naive/src/functions/activities.json, beside the tool catalog and on its process groups. An activity is a unit of work (APQC level 4) written as an O*NET task statement: one sentence that starts with a verb, at most 30 words. Each activity is filed under an APQC level 2 process group from tools.json, optionally a level 3 process, and is cross-industry or for one NAICS industry. It may cite the source it comes from and may be scored on seven published scales the catalog lists with their ranges: the CDR taxonomy's regulatory restriction, physical deployment and cognitive complexity, the RL feasibility index's verification, and O*NET's importance, share and frequency. A scored activity names who rated it, when and on what basis. Scores are one rater's judgment in a version 0.x, unevaluated catalog, and they never decide anything; the most a score may do is propose an open decision for a person. check-activities.ts checks the catalog. Tools.json and its schema are unchanged.
decisions.why: A workflow step says what an agent does but not which unit of work that is, so nothing tells a function how regulated, physical or checkable its work is. SciNet (Alamos and Althoff 2026) showed the method on research work: task statements in O*NET form, added and checked one at a time, placed on a work axis and a context axis, and scored on the CDR, RL feasibility and O*NET scales. APQC's framework already gives Naive its functions and process groups (EE-047, EE-163), and its level 4 is the activity, so the catalog files activities under the groups Naive has. Keeping the catalog in its own file leaves the tool catalog's schema, which a console copies, as it was.

decisions.decision: Naive carries APQC's Process Classification Framework 8.0, cross-industry, levels 1 to 5, as data in packages/naive/src/functions/pcf.json: each element's hierarchy id, its name verbatim from APQC and its five-digit element id, with the attribution APQC's licence requires in every copy, and none of APQC's definitions or measures. scripts/import-pcf.ts writes the elements from a hierarchy extracted from APQC's own files, and check-pcf.ts checks them. Hierarchy ids change between PCF versions and element ids do not, so a reference meant to outlast a version uses the element id. Element ids are not required to be unique, because APQC files a few at two hierarchy ids. An activity's optional process must be a level 3 element of pcf.json. The tool catalog is still on PCF 7.4 names and numbers; moving it to 8.0 is a separate change and is not built, and check-pcf.ts --json lists the drift without failing.
decisions.why: The activity catalog (EE-164) let an activity name a level 3 process with nothing to check it against, because Naive had no PCF data and had not read APQC's terms. APQC's 13 Definitions and Key Measures articles for version 8.0 (March 2026) print the licence: a perpetual, worldwide, royalty-free license to use, copy, publish, modify, and create derivative works of the PCF, provided every copy and derivative work contains APQC's attribution. With the data and the terms in hand, Naive can ship the hierarchy and check references to it. APQC already defines the activity and task levels, so the activity catalog keeps only the activities Naive adds. Keeping the PCF in its own file leaves tools.json and its schema, which a console copies, unchanged.

decisions.decision: The tool catalog (packages/naive/src/functions/tools.json) uses APQC's Process Classification Framework 8.0 for its process groups: the hierarchy ids, names and element ids of pcf.json's level 2, all 74. Against PCF 7.4, 5.3 Deliver service to customer is 5.4, 13.6 to 13.9 are 13.7 to 13.10, 3.2 has a new element id, 7.1 and 7.3 take APQC's 8.0 wording and the 26 groups that had no element id have one. The two process groups new in 8.0 get no new tool: 5.3 Manage and Operate Service Delivery System is served by Engagements and 13.6 Manage Content by Knowledge base. check-pcf.ts fails when a process group in tools.json is not a level 2 element of pcf.json, when its name or element id differs, or when tools.json lacks one. The catalog's version is 0.2.0. A console that keeps a copy of tools.json copies it again.
decisions.why: EE-165 shipped PCF 8.0 beside a tool catalog on PCF 7.4, so the same id meant two process groups: 13.9 was Manage sustainability in tools.json and Manage environmental health and safety in pcf.json, and an activity's process could be checked against its own level only. One version in both files removes that. Holding tools.json to pcf.json in a check keeps APQC's names from being written by hand again. Giving the two new groups to existing tools avoids inventing tools nobody asked for; a tool of their own can be added when a business needs one.

decisions.decision: The activity catalog's first activities are taken from SciNet v1.10.0 (CC BY 4.0) by scripts/import-scinet.ts: the Data Gathering and Data Analysis tasks of the subfields Entrepreneurship & Innovation and Marketing, and the universal task of obtaining ethical approval and informed consent, 38 in all, filed cross-industry under APQC process group 3.1 Understand markets, customers, and capabilities and its process 3.1.1 Perform customer and market intelligence analysis. Each keeps SciNet's statement, names SciNet and the task's place in it as its source, and carries SciNet's scores on the catalog's scales with rated.by SciNet and a basis that says the scores rate the task as researchers perform it and not as a business does. The script selects by subfield, category and named universal task, replaces only SciNet's activities under the process group it is given, and writes the same bytes on a rerun. SciNet's files are not kept in the repository. A person reviews which activities enter before the seed merges.
decisions.why: Naive has no Research function, and the work SciNet describes that a venture also does is market and customer research, which APQC files under 3.1. SciNet's entrepreneurship and marketing tasks are the closest published, scored task statements to that work, so they test the catalog with real data instead of statements written for the purpose. Their scores were given for academic researchers, so they are carried as SciNet's judgment and labelled, never as a rating of a business. A script with a fixed selection makes the seed repeatable when SciNet releases again and keeps hand edits out of the file.

decisions.decision: A step of a function workflow may name the activity it performs, in an optional field activity: the hierarchy id of an APQC level 4 activity in packages/naive/src/functions/pcf.json, or the id of an activity in packages/naive/src/functions/activities.json. check-functions.ts fails when the id is in neither file or sits under an APQC category other than the function's. The field is optional, and no step is required to name one. Two steps of the marketing and sales workflows name APQC activities as the first use: asking for the pipeline is 3.5.1.2 Identify/receive leads/opportunities, and checking stages is 3.5.1.6 Manage opportunity pipeline.
decisions.why: A workflow step is Naive's own unit below APQC's levels, the work an agent does to perform an activity. Without the link, a score on an activity has no path to the step an agent runs, so nothing could later propose who does a step or how it is verified. APQC already names 1,352 activities, so a step names APQC's where one fits and a catalog activity only where Naive added one. Keeping the field optional lets workflows adopt it one at a time.

decisions.decision: The activity catalog's scores propose decisions through proposal rules kept as data in packages/naive/src/functions/activities.json. A rule is a list of lines on scales, a question for a person and the basis for its lines. For each function a venture lists in venture.json departments, a rule picks the rated cross-industry activities under that function's process groups whose scores meet every line, and naive activities propose files one open decision per rule and function, activity-<rule>-<function>, through the decision door as the agent activity-proposals. naive activities list shows the same and writes nothing. A rerun leaves a decision already filed, open or decided, as it is. The first two rules ask whether an agent performs activities whose result can be checked and whether a person approves restricted activities. Their lines are unvalidated priors.
decisions.why: EE-164 says a score never decides and may at most propose an open decision for a person, and until now nothing read the scores. Keeping the lines in the catalog as data, and not in code, lets a person change them in one reviewed place and lets the check hold them to the scales. One decision per rule and function keeps the docket short: 38 activities give two decisions, not 38. Filing through the decision door means the proposal is drafted by an agent, logged in provenance and waits for a person, like every other proposal in Naive. The scores are SciNet's, for researchers, so the note of every proposal says who rated each activity and on what basis.

decisions.decision: A venture sets its own lines for the activity catalog's proposal rules in naive.config.json. activity_proposals.rules maps a rule id to off, so the rule proposes nothing in that venture, or to { when }, lines that replace all of the catalog's for that rule. A rule left out keeps the catalog's lines. The decision a rule files keeps its id, and its note says the lines are the venture's. check-config and naive activities refuse a rule id the catalog lacks, a scale it does not list, a line outside the scale's range and lines no score meets. Proposing a venture's lines from its market and industry is not built.
decisions.why: EE-169 kept the lines in the catalog and called them unvalidated priors. Where a line should sit depends on the venture: a regulated business wants a person's approval at a lower restriction score than the catalog asks, and a venture with no agents has no use for the question of what an agent may do. A threshold is contextual to a venture's market, industry and time, so it is the venture's to set and never fixed in code. Replacing all of a rule's lines, and not merging them scale by scale, keeps what a venture wrote the whole of what applies. Holding the venture's lines to the catalog's rule ids and scales means a typing mistake fails the check and does not silently propose nothing.

decisions.decision: An activity the catalog files for one NAICS industry applies to a venture when the NAICS code in venture.json industry starts with the activity's code. A two-digit code in one of the three sectors NAICS numbers with a range (31-33, 44-45, 48-49) names the whole sector. A venture with no industry gets the cross-industry activities only. An industry activity is proposed in the same decision as the cross-industry activities of its rule and function, and the note names its NAICS code. The catalog holds no industry activity yet.
decisions.why: EE-164 gave an activity a scope, cross-industry or one NAICS industry, and EE-169 left the industry ones out of proposals because nothing matched them to a venture. venture.json already records the venture's industry as a NAICS code. NAICS is hierarchical by prefix, so a prefix test is the standard reading of membership, with the three ranged sectors as its one exception. Keeping industry activities in the same decision keeps the docket to one decision per rule and function.

decisions.decision: A person's answer to an activity proposal is applied through the decision's own merge. A proposal rule may name what its answer sets: a field of the venture's activity assignments, operations/activity-assignments.json, either performer (agent or person) or approval (person or none). The decision the rule files offers that field's values as its options and names one applies_to field per activity found. A person decides, and merging the decided answer writes it for each activity after checking the file against its schema, so an answer outside the options is refused. The record type is activity-assignments. Nothing reads the assignments yet.
decisions.why: EE-169 let scores propose a decision, and a person's answer to it changed nothing. Decisions already have applies_to and a merge that is separate from approving, can be delegated, is checked against the target's schema and is logged in provenance, so applying an answer needs no new mechanism, only a record to write to and a rule that says which field. Taking the options from the assignments schema keeps one list of allowed values. A person still decides and a person still merges, so a score never changes who does the work.

decisions.decision: A venture's activity assignments reach the agent through its brief. The brief of a function agent in a venture carries the catalog activities under its function's process groups that the venture has assigned, each with who performs it, whether a person approves it and the rule that follows in plain sentences, and a workflow step that names an assigned activity carries the same rule. Where a person performs the activity the agent asks or hands it over and does not perform it. Where a person approves it the agent raises the result as a decision and does not treat the activity as done until a person decides. The gate does not enforce an assignment.
decisions.why: EE-172 wrote a person's answer to a file that nothing read. An agent acts from its brief, which every harness reads through the MCP server and naive agent, so the brief is the one place where an assignment changes what an agent does without a new runner. The gate cannot enforce it, because a write names a route and not the activity it is for, and guessing the activity from the route would refuse work a person never restricted. Saying the rule in the brief and saying plainly that it is not enforced keeps the docs true.

decisions.decision: A working copy that was offline syncs with its business store by pull and push, and conflicting edits merge field by field. Pull fetches what changed since the sync point and merges each record from its base, local and store copies; push sends each change with its base version and is refused whole if the store moved. A field changed on one side lands without asking. The same field changed to different values on both sides is a conflict: the record keeps the store's value and a person decides between both values, never the sync and never an agent. Files are addressed by their sha256 and never conflict. The field merge is built as packages/naive/src/engine/merge.ts. Not built: filing a conflict as a decision, provenance re-chaining, the host's sync API, device sign-in and naive sync.
decisions.why: Torian, 2026-11-25 06:21Z: a founder working offline must be able to sync what they changed with their database. On a decision card at 06:26Z he chose field merge with conflicts as decisions over last writer wins, which silently loses work, and CRDTs, which are heavy for small JSON records. Keeping both values and asking a person matches Naive's rule that agents propose and people decide. The design is docs/design/OFFLINE_SYNC_2026-11-25.md.

decisions.decision: A conflict offline sync finds is an ordinary decision. It is proposed once by the agent sync, carries sync_conflict in the decision record (the file, the path, the base, local and store values and who wrote each) and stays open while the record keeps the store's value. A person approves store, local or a value of their own written as JSON, and merging the decided version writes that value at the path, checked against the record's schema and logged in provenance like any merge. Resolving a conflict over a whole record from a decision is not built.
decisions.why: EE-174 says a person decides every same-field conflict and nothing is lost. Naive already has one door for that: an agent proposes, a person approves, a merge applies the answer (EE-058). Using it means conflicts appear in the decision queue and console like every other decision, and need no second approval path. applies_to writes a string at a dotted field, which cannot hold a number, an object or an item of a list by id, so the conflict carries its own path and values.

decisions.decision: A venture's activity assignments may name an APQC level 4 activity by its hierarchy id, as well as an activity in the activity catalog. These are the same two forms a workflow step's activity takes. A person writes such an assignment through the record's route. No proposal rule covers APQC activities and a decision's merge does not set one. Nothing above level 4 can be assigned.
decisions.why: EE-173 marks a workflow step whose activity is assigned, and every shipped step that names an activity names an APQC activity, which the assignments could not hold. So the marking never applied. Accepting the id a step already uses makes it apply with no new record. Proposals stay with the catalog because APQC activities carry no scores, and a score is what a rule reads. Levels 1 to 3 are left out because who holds them is still being decided.

decisions.decision: A push writes a working copy's provenance lines again on top of the business store's chain, as a rebase writes a commit again on top of another branch. A re-chained line keeps its own time, entity, activity, agent and sha256, so the push does not claim the write; only prev and hash are the store chain's, and the line carries rechained_from with the hash and prev it had in the working copy's log and the id of that working copy. Keeping the original prev makes the original hash checkable from the line alone, so packages/naive/src/checks/check-provenance.ts accepts a re-chained line only when the block names an original hash, an original prev and a working copy, and the original hash is this line as the working copy wrote it. The pure function is packages/naive/src/core/rechain.ts. Re-chaining a line that was already re-chained is refused. The lines a push sends are a subsequence of the working copy's log, because a push leaves out the lines about records it does not sync (EE-178), so each line is checked by its own hash over its own prev and never against the line sent before it. A working copy's own chain stays in that working copy: a store proves each line as the working copy wrote it, not the order it wrote them in.
decisions.why: EE-174 says a working copy is a full business and every offline write goes into its local provenance log (EE-031). Those lines chain onto each other, so they cannot be appended to the store's chain as they are: their prev names a line the store does not have. Appending them unchanged would break the store's chain, and dropping them would lose who wrote what offline. Writing them again on top of the store tip keeps the chain checkable and keeps the writes, which is what git does on a rebase. The block names its original hash so nothing is silently rewritten in the move, and its original prev so a checker can recompute that hash with nothing but the line. The design is docs/design/OFFLINE_SYNC_2026-11-25.md, section Provenance.

decisions.decision: The offline sync client is `naive sync link|pull|push|status` over one engine module, packages/naive/src/engine/sync.ts. A working copy keeps its own sync state in .naive/sync.json: the host, the business, this copy's id, the sync point and the base version and base content hash of each record. Pull merges base, local and store with mergeRecord, takes the base content from the blob store by that hash, writes each merged record with a provenance line, files each same-field conflict with fileConflicts, copies down the files records name by sha256, and moves the point last; a merge that brought local fields in must still pass the record's schema, or the store's value stands and a decision holds the local one. Push sends every record whose bytes differ from its base, each with its base version, uploads the file hashes the host is missing first, carries the provenance lines the host does not have, and on a 409 pulls, merges and retries at most twice. One filter, syncable(path), governs both directions: a JSON record the data model owns that a record route takes writes for, so no log, no derived file, no .env file, nothing under .naive/, _eval/ or _private/, no record marked private or sensitive, and not venture.json, which no route claims. A device sign-in token lives in the operating system's keychain (security on macOS, secret-tool on Linux) or in ~/.config/naive/credentials.json with mode 0600, never in the business folder. The host comes from --host or sync.host in naive.config.json, the HTTP client is injectable, and every command is refused when NAIVE_RUNTIME=hosted.
decisions.why: EE-174 settled how a working copy and a business store come back together; this is the client half, and the choices it had to make. The base content comes from the blob store because that is where every write already puts the bytes its provenance line names (EE-031), so a three-way merge needs no second copy. The base is always the store's content at the version last seen, even after a merge, so the next merge asks the right question. The sync state is derived and local to one copy, so it is never synced and a full pull rebuilds it. Records changed are found by hashing bytes rather than by a dirty list, so a pull or push that stopped halfway converges on a rerun and a pull after a pull writes nothing. The data model already says which paths are records, which are logs and which are derived, and the route table already says which of those a route takes writes for, so the filter reads both instead of keeping a second list that could drift; the host writes each accepted change through its own router, so a path no route claims would be refused whole, and the two ends agree by construction. The explicit never-send list is the guard for the paths the data model does call records inside .naive/ and _eval/. The same filter guards what a pull writes, so a host cannot push a path into a working copy that the working copy would never send. The token is in the keychain because a business folder is in git. Naive names no vendor, so there is no default host. Hosted mode is refused because a hosted store is the store.

decisions.decision: Work is split between a person and agents by the kind of an activity and not by its APQC level. A person performs four kinds at any level: a decision, a value, a commitment and a relationship. Agents perform the rest. APQC levels 1 and 2 become the briefing a person reads (not built). The activity catalog holds the kinds as data (kinds in packages/naive/src/functions/activities.json): a kind is told from the verb and the terms of an activity's statement, or of an APQC level 4 activity's name, and the first kind with a clause the statement meets is the activity's kind (packages/naive/src/engine/activity-kinds.ts). An activity a venture has not assigned takes its kind's default, so a function agent's brief and a step that names the activity say a person performs it, marked default with the kind. A venture's own assignment in operations/activity-assignments.json replaces a default. The words that mark a kind are unvalidated priors, and naive activities defaults lists every activity that has one.
decisions.why: Torian chose this on a decision card on 2026-11-25, over the alternative that the person owns levels 1 and 2 and agents perform level 3 and below. Level 4 holds decisions that matter, such as approving a price, hiring a candidate and negotiating a contract, so a line drawn at a level would hand those to agents. A default by kind means a business that has assigned nothing still keeps those with a person. The kinds are data and not code so a person can read and change the words, and a default is marked as one so nobody mistakes it for a person's decision about that business.

decisions.decision: APQC levels 1 and 2 are the briefing a person reads about a venture's activities. naive activities briefing (packages/naive/src/engine/activity-briefing.ts) gives one entry per function the venture lists, with its APQC category, and under it each process group: the activities a person performs, the activities an agent performs and a person approves, each from the venture's own assignment or by default from the activity's kind (EE-179), and how many activities are left to the function's agent. It reads the venture's assignments, the activity catalog and the framework, and writes nothing. No record holds a briefing and nothing is assigned at level 1, 2 or 3: a briefing is derived from the level 4 assignments and defaults each time it is read. Open decisions, handoffs and results are not in the briefing (not built).
decisions.why: EE-179 split work by the kind of an activity and made levels 1 and 2 the briefing layer. A person running a business cannot read 1,352 activities, and does not need to: 13 categories and 74 process groups fit on a page, and each group can say what it needs from them. Deriving the briefing keeps one source of truth, the level 4 assignments and the kinds, so a briefing cannot disagree with what the agents were told.

decisions.decision: A workflow step is required, or one to consider. A step with `consider` (function-workflow.schema.json) says `why` a person might want it and, optionally, `when` the agent runs it unasked. The agent runs a step to consider only when its `when` holds or a person asks, and otherwise reports that it considered the step and why it did not run it. A step without `consider` is required: the agent runs it or raises a decision. Every workflow has at least one required step (check-functions.ts). The briefing a person reads (EE-180) lists each function's steps to consider. No shipped workflow has a step to consider yet, nothing evaluates `when`, which is a sentence the agent reads, and nothing records that a step was considered.
decisions.why: Running Naive on Naive on 2026-11-25 showed every function has work that fits some businesses or phases and not others, such as a competitive pricing review before there is a price. A step had no way to say so, so an agent either ran everything or the work was left out of the workflow. The founder asked that such work be activities or questions to consider, not mandatory tasks.

decisions.decision: A function workflow is due by its trigger. `naive due` (packages/naive/src/engine/due.ts) reads the trigger of every workflow of the functions a venture lists, the venture's run log (`.naive/workflow-runs.jsonl`) and its provenance log, and says which workflows are due now and why: intake until it has finished once, a schedule when its cadence has passed since its last finished run, an event when a record on its route went live since then (a draft held for a person does not count), and a request never on its own. A failed run does not move a schedule. `naive due record` appends a run. Each entry says whether the venture's phase lists the workflow as active. Nothing starts a due workflow: the loop that does is not built, the run log is not synced, and it is not a record a route serves.
decisions.why: All 31 shipped workflows declared a trigger and no code read it, so a weekly review was weekly only on paper. The founder asked on 2026-11-25 for hooks and loops across all 13 functions with a clear statement of what triggers each. Saying what is due, from data already declared, comes before a runner that acts on it.

decisions.decision: The loop starts due function workflows as far as a mode allows. `naive loop` (packages/naive/src/engine/loop.ts) reads what `naive due` says and the mode under `loops` in naive.config.json: `mode` for the venture, `functions` per function and `workflows` per workflow, the most specific winning. manual, the default, starts nothing. ask files one open decision per due occurrence with the options start and skip, starts on start and records a skipped run on skip. auto starts the workflow as its function agent through NAIVE_AGENT_CMD and records the run as done or failed. No mode goes past the gate: there is no bypass mode, and a one-way door stays a person's. A workflow the phase does not list as active is left alone unless a mode names it. A workflow whose last run failed is asked about before it starts again. Only a person sets a mode. `naive loop plan` writes nothing, `tick` acts once under a lock file, and `watch` ticks on Effect's Schedule.spaced. Modes per time box, retries inside a tick and a watch that survives a restart are not built.
decisions.why: The founder asked on 2026-11-26 for modes like the ones AI tools have, proactive for some functions and patient for others, built on the two-way doors already in Naive, and said a draft must not spin up the next records until he approves it. A mode decides only whether the loop starts an agent. The gate, drafts and decision rights already decide what that agent may write, so the loop adds no second permission system.

decisions.decision: Every workspace and venture record type in the data model names `data`, what its records are to the business in data management's terms: master (a lasting fact kept as one current record that is edited), reference (a list or setting other records are read against), transactional (one event or one piece of work at a time, which accumulates) or derived (computed from other records, never a source of truth). packages/naive/src/checks/check-data-model.ts requires it on those types, holds a log to transactional, and `dataOf` in packages/naive/src/records/index.ts reads it. It is separate from `kind` (record, log or derived), which says how a host commits the file. An app's record types may leave it out. The first classification of the 119 types is the agent's and a person may change any line. Nothing else reads it yet.
decisions.why: The founder asked on 2026-11-26 whether the hooks and loops plan accounts for golden records and transactional records. Naive had a customer master schema and logs, and no field that says which of its record types are the business's lasting facts and which are events. The element state and quality steps need that: an element's master records say whether it is present and current, and its transactional records are evidence that it operates.

decisions.decision: A person withdraws an open or deferred decision with `mentura withdraw <decision> --by <person>`, and with `--duplicate-of <other>` marks it as asking again what another decision asks. The record keeps `duplicate_of`, `withdrawn_by` and `withdrawn_at`, its status becomes withdrawn, so it leaves the queue, and the withdrawal is a provenance line. Only a person withdraws: an agent proposes and never removes a question, and the function agents, researchers and role templates count as roles, not people, for approving and withdrawing. A decided decision changes by a new version, not a withdrawal. The decision it duplicates must exist, be another one, and still ask the question. The matrix reports a duplicate that is not withdrawn or names no decision.
decisions.why: The run of Naive on itself on 2026-11-25 asked who owns the business three times, in three decisions from three functions with options that did not line up, and Naive had no way to keep one and set the others aside. A person had to answer the same question three times or leave two open forever.

decisions.decision: A campaign or a sprint is a time box, a venture record type `time-box` at operations/time-boxes/<id>.json (route operations/time-box/[id]), in the operations layer with function null, data transactional and writer person. It names its kind (campaign or sprint), a goal, `starts`, `ends`, a status (active, closed or cancelled), the functions or workflows it covers and an optional `loop_mode`, which requires `set_by`. It is open while active, from `starts` until `ends`. A function workflow's trigger may say `during` a campaign or a sprint: then it is due only while such a time box covers it, and an event counts only from the time box's start (packages/naive/src/engine/due.ts). An open time box's loop mode applies to the workflows it covers, below a mode set for a workflow by name and above the function's and the venture's, and only with a person in `set_by` (packages/naive/src/engine/loop.ts). The shipped workflow marketing-and-sales/campaign-daily-review runs daily during a campaign. A time box's measures, a check that it names workflows the venture has, and a command to open or close one are not built.
decisions.why: The founder asked on 2026-11-26 whether the hooks and loops plan handles campaigns and sprints, and wanted some work proactive and some patient. A campaign or sprint is bounded work with its own pace: work that only makes sense while it runs, and a mode a person picks for that stretch, which ends when it ends.

decisions.decision: Each element of APQC's framework that a venture runs has one accountable owner, the A of RACI: a role or a person. packages/naive/src/engine/element-owners.ts resolves it by the first rule that applies: an owner the venture names in operations/element-owners.json (record type element-owners, per hierarchy id { role } or { person }); else, for an activity a person performs or approves by the venture's assignment (EE-172, EE-176) or by its kind (EE-179), the delegation root when the owner it would inherit is an agent; else the parent's owner; else, for a category the venture lists in venture.json departments, its function's agent. The owner is not the performer. A role is a role template, the venture's own or Naive's, or a function agent, and it answers only within its reach: a lead's portfolio, a role's one function, or anywhere for a role of function all. `naive owners` lists each element with its owner, kind and source, and packages/naive/src/checks/check-owners.ts fails on an element left unowned and on an owner that names no role or answers outside its reach.
decisions.why: The founder asked on 2026-11-25 to assign each element to a person or an agent and to know who is accountable. Naive said who performs an activity and whether a person approves it, and nothing above an activity. An agent does not answer for work a person performs, so such an activity goes to the person who holds what is not delegated, the delegation root, unless the venture names its owner.

decisions.decision: The element graph is derived from the function workflows and the route table, not stored. Its nodes are APQC elements (the 13 functions, every activity a workflow step names, and their ancestors, a catalog activity under its process or process group), the workflows, the route patterns they name and the record types those routes resolve to. Its edges are contains (the PCF hierarchy), belongs-to (a workflow to its function's category), performs (a step to its activity), writes (a step to a route), reads (a workflow to a route), listens (an event trigger to its route), resolves (a route to a record type) and the derived feeds: element A feeds element B of the same level when a route a step attached to A writes resolves to a record type that a workflow attached to B reads or is triggered by, and each feed names its evidence (writer workflow and step, the route written, reader workflow, the route read, read or trigger, and the record type). A step is attached to its activity, every ancestor of it and its function's category. A workflow reading what it wrote itself is a loop, not a feed. packages/naive/src/engine/element-graph.ts builds it with Effect's Graph module as a pure, deterministic function, answers upstream, downstream, the routes read that no workflow writes and the routes written that none reads, and `naive graph` prints it. No record type and no schema change.
decisions.why: Step 6 of the hooks and loops design (docs/design/HOOKS_AND_LOOPS_2026-11-26.md). Step 7 needs to know what each element feeds before it can say what an absent or weak element does to others, and the workflows already declare what they read and write, so the edges can be read off them instead of being kept by hand where they would drift.

decisions.decision: Naive ships a rubric for judging which programming language fits a system, as data in packages/naive/src/functions/it/language-rubric.json (record type language-rubric, schema packages/naive/src/records/language-rubric.schema.json). It has eight criteria: runtime fit, correctness, the concurrency and effect model, ecosystem, interop with Naive, team skill, operability and licence. Each has a question, why, described levels on a 0 to 4 scale, the ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics it serves and its sources as reference ids in the operations layer's references, and a default weight that is an unvalidated prior; the weights sum to 1. Runtime fit and licence are gates: a 0 rules a candidate out. A system may set its own weights and must-haves. The pure scorer scoreLanguages in packages/naive/src/engine/language-rubric.ts rules out a candidate on a gate or a must-have whatever its other scores, ranks the rest by weighted total, reports totals within the tie band as tied, and says a person decides. Naive's own choices are worked examples: TypeScript on Effect for the framework (EE-087, EE-125, EE-159) and Lean 4 for proofs (EE-095); their scores are the agent's judgment from those decisions and a person may change any. packages/naive/src/checks/check-language-rubric.ts checks the rubric across files. The tool-selection skill says when to use it. No command and no route serve it.
decisions.why: The founder asked that Naive be built on Effect in TypeScript and that there be a way to judge which language fits a system. docs/design/HOOKS_AND_LOOPS_2026-11-26.md listed the rubric as not written.

decisions.decision: An element's state, quality and effects are derived, not stored. State is a statechart with five states (absent, started, operating, degraded, retired) as a tagged union and a pure, total transition function over eight events (record written with its data category, run finished, run failed, run overdue, record stale, upstream down, cause cleared, retire); degraded keeps its causes and the state it left and returns there when the last cause clears, and retired is absorbing. Each element's own state replays its live provenance writes to its record types, its workflows' runs, and at now its overdue schedules and stale records. Quality is a capability level after ISO/IEC 33020 read only from evidence Naive keeps and capped at 3, with the run counts behind levels 2 and 3 labelled unvalidated priors; levels 4 and 5 need element measures Naive does not keep. Effects propagate over the feeds edges of the element graph (EE-188): every feed is a need, an absent, retired or degraded upstream degrades every started, operating or degraded element it feeds with the cause named, and a level is capped at the weakest upstream level plus a slack of 1 (an unvalidated prior), to the least fixpoint, which terminates because each round climbs a finite lattice. packages/naive/src/engine/element-state.ts holds the pure rules for the Lean proofs of step 8, packages/naive/src/engine/element-effects.ts reads a venture into them, and `naive effects` prints each element or one element's what-if. No record type and no schema change.
decisions.why: Step 7 of the hooks and loops design (docs/design/HOOKS_AND_LOOPS_2026-11-26.md). Torian asked to know, for each element, what state it is in, what its quality is and what happens to other elements when it is absent, weak or strong, and to test and formally verify that. Deriving from the logs Naive already keeps avoids a second store that could drift, and keeping the transition and propagation pure and small lets step 8 state them in Lean 4 without Mathlib.

decisions.decision: The four data labels sourced, estimated, synthetic and gold are EE-095 terms over a record's facts, with the theorems in packages/naive/lean/Naive/Labels.lean. Gold needs a person's acceptance and one of our own ventures. A synthetic record is never under any venture. No check reads the label a record declares.
decisions.why: Torian approved this vocabulary on 2026-11-26, and gold comes only from our own ventures. A later check can judge a record's declared label from these facts.

decisions.decision: A raw source is written with its text in one write, create-only, and the router sets sha256 from the text. A second write to the same id is refused, and a write whose text hashes to a source already in the venture is refused, naming that source. The allowed-source term refuses a host on the closed deny list (linkedin.com, www.linkedin.com, g2.com, www.g2.com) and a fetch the input says used a login.
decisions.why: Free public data only (Torian, 2026-11-26). No LinkedIn scraping (Torian). G2's terms ban scrapers. Raw is immutable (EE-070). A source without its text failed naive check.

decisions.decision: Every APQC citation is judged by the pcf-citation term. A citation passes only when its element id is in packages/naive/src/functions/pcf.json, the cited name is that element's name, and the cited version is that file's version. The theorem citation_needs_element says a citation whose element id is not in the PCF does not pass. departments.json cites each category by its 8.0 name and element id, and the six APQC standards in ontology.json cite PCF 8.0. Pricing is 3.2.3 Define pricing strategy (element 10123) and 3.2.3.4 Approve pricing strategies/policies and targets (element 10125). check-pcf.ts (EE-165) and check-tools.ts (EE-166) still compare ids with pcf.json as plain checks. That is debt. Those two checks should move onto this term, and this decision does not move them.
decisions.why: Torian's rule, recorded as Q6 on 2026-11-26: an id or label membership check goes through EE-095 and Lean. The department name for 7.0 and six ontology standards still cited PCF 7.4, and the pricing citation named 3.2.2, which in 8.0 is brands.

decisions.decision: Founder templates and synthetic exemplars made from public inputs live in Naive, which is public. Gold exemplars, and anything seeded from gold or from a run venture, live in Dogfood, which is private. A synthetic exemplar in Naive passes synthetic-record and declares that label. Each source it cites passes allowed-source, and none is a Dogfood path or a run venture. An eval file has one fixed canary and items. A held-out item passes held-out-item: the split is held-out, and the id is in no exemplar file and no prompt fixture. A label is non-null only when labelled_by names a person, judged by person-label. The faithful-author term is not on main, so person-label states that rule in this change.
decisions.why: Torian decided this split on 2026-11-26 (Q5 in docs/design/OBSERVED_VENTURES_2026-11-26.md). Gold comes from our own ventures and can hold private data. Synthetic data keeps the statistical traits of its seed (NIST SP 800-188), so a synthetic exemplar seeded from gold stays private too.

decisions.decision: A meeting is a venture record type `meeting` at operations/meetings/<id>.json (route operations/meeting/[id]), in the operations layer with function null, data transactional and writer any, so the gate and the team plan decide who writes it. It states a goal and the outcome that shows the goal was reached before it opens, names who called it and who attends (people and agents), and holds an agenda worked in order. A meeting may walk a function workflow (`workflow`, `<function>/<workflow>`), one agenda item per step. Each item is pending, done, skipped (to loop back to) or handed-off (to an agent or person to recommend or finish). Its status is planned, open, closed or abandoned; an open meeting has `opened_at`, and a closed one has its outcome, `closed_at` and no pending item. It keeps minutes, the outcome (records, decisions, handoffs, follow-up), what each attendee takes away and how it was recorded. Closed meetings are an app's shared memory for its agents; Naive copies a meeting into no second record. A command that runs a meeting is not built in Naive: Mentura's agent runtime runs one.
decisions.why: The founder asked on 2026-11-26 to work through each function's workflow in order with agents as if in a meeting, with defined goals and outcomes, stored so every agent can read the record and have its memory updated, and with skipped steps looped back to or handed to an agent for its recommendation.

decisions.decision: An undecided record holds several ideas at once. A decision record carries candidates, each one idea for the record it decides: an id, a label, a why, who proposed it, what it rests on, and either body, the whole proposed record, or patch, the fields it proposes. Any number coexist while the decision is open, so a goal or a requirement, a record type with no options of its own, keeps every idea in play. An agent or a person adds one with mentura option add; each live candidate's id is an option beside the strings in options, and only a person chooses one. Deciding with a candidate's id makes merge write that candidate, schema-checked first, and the ideas not chosen stay on the decision. Withdrawing is a person's and is one command for either: mentura withdraw <decision> takes the question off the table and --option <id> takes one idea, leaving the decision open. Nothing is ever removed, so both stay recoverable: a withdrawn candidate keeps who withdrew it and why, and a person adding its id again puts it back. Decisions are fluid: mentura reopen is a person's, free while the venture is in Discovery or Validation, and past Validation or for a one-way door only with an explicit override that the record keeps, a one-way door also only by a founder. A reopened decision keeps its decided version in versions, so a rollback restores the answer. A single record's route read carries undecided, every decision still open over it with every live idea, so an agent reads all the options instead of guessing one. This is not mentura accept --pick, which chooses between rival drafts of one record that the gate held and removes the others; candidates are named, reasoned ideas inside the decision that survive the choice, and optionsOf returns a variants decision's options strings and a decision's live candidate ids in one list, so one call answers what can be chosen on any decision.
decisions.why: Torian decided this on 2026-11-26: options must stay open until the right time, especially in Discovery and Validation, and decisions must be easy to change or withdraw. A triage run of his message found that only decisions have options, so a goal or a requirement could hold one idea at a time, and that no route deletes anything, so taking an idea off the table had to be a withdrawal that keeps it rather than a delete. Only a person decides, so an agent adds ideas and never chooses, reopens or withdraws one.

decisions.decision: A goal is a durable record, like the decision ledger. goal.schema.json carries a status (proposed, active, met, missed, dropped, superseded; a record with no status is proposed, so every goal written before this stays valid), who set it and when, the goal it serves (parent), the goals it replaces (supersedes, superseded_by), a due date, where it came from (sources) and the result it was settled on. The lifecycle is a state machine in packages/naive/src/engine/goals.ts: proposed to active, dropped or superseded; active to met, missed, dropped or superseded; a settled goal reopens only to active, so a mis-set status is corrected and never overwritten, and a goal nobody adopted is never met or missed. Only a person settles a goal: naive goals status refuses anyone who is not a person of the venture and an agent acting as one, and the router holds an agent's write of a lifecycle field as a draft whatever the gate says, the same rule EE-058 gives a write that settles a decision, so a person's acceptance is what puts it live. An agent that rewords a goal a person adopted is refused and told to write a new goal that supersedes it. History needs no new log: every version is already in provenance.jsonl with its bytes in the blob store, so naive goals history and naive goals show --at read them back. naive goals list shows the goals waiting as held drafts, marked as drafts. packages/naive/src/checks/check-goals.ts checks what crosses records: parents, successors, results, active goals, and requirements that derive from a goal that is no longer live.
decisions.why: Torian decided on 2026-11-26 that his ventures are validated through a structured workflow in which goals are set first and then kept, so goals must be durable objects like the decision ledger, with a lifecycle and a history, and decisions must stay easy to change or withdraw. Only a person decides, so an agent proposes a goal and its status change waits as a draft.

decisions.decision: A risk's impact range cites a source or is marked an estimate, and expected loss carries the same label. packages/naive/src/records/risk.schema.json gives the impact exactly one of `source` (what the range rests on: a record route or a reference id, as the finance function's figures name theirs, and never text that starts with assumption) or `estimate` (`basis`, how the range was reached, and `by`, the person or agent role that estimated it), and refuses neither or both. `expectedLoss` in packages/naive/src/engine/generators/risk.ts returns the impact's `source` or `estimate` beside the range. The legal package moves to 0.4.0, and its migration `risk-impact-label` escalates each existing risk whose impact has neither, by file, and writes nothing. No check resolves a source to a record or reference that exists.
decisions.why: Torian decided on 2026-11-26 that the finance function's rule holds for risks too: the finance agent cites a record for every figure it writes, and a number with no source is a guess that says so (packages/naive/src/functions/finance/agent.md). The risk register required a money range with no field saying where it came from, and expected loss computed from it read as a fact. A structured estimate names who made it because an agent or a person may write a risk.

decisions.decision: Naive recommends tools per goal and per activity, and the recommendation favours tools that give the system visibility of the activity and tools the venture owns. The visibility rubric is data (packages/naive/src/functions/it/visibility-rubric.json): five criteria, each with a question, why it matters, described levels on a 0 to 4 scale, its sources and a default weight that is an unvalidated prior a venture overrides under visibility in naive.config.json. The weights are activity-record 0.3, ownership 0.25, export-and-api 0.2, events 0.15 and consent-and-retention 0.1, so visibility carries 0.65 and ownership 0.25. consent-and-retention is a gate: a 0 rules a candidate out, because recording a person needs a lawful basis, a retention period and a way to erase (GDPR articles 5, 6, 7, 13 and 17). activity-record is not a gate: a 0 means the tool leaves the activity unrecorded, which is reported as a blind spot and still ranked, because only a person rules a tool out. The rubric also names the channel an activity is performed on, read from the words of its statement as an activity's kind is (EE-179), and the tool kinds that capture each channel, named as kinds and never as vendors. scoreTools in packages/naive/src/engine/visibility-rubric.ts is the pure scorer, and naive tools recommend [--goal <id>] [--activity <id>] [--function <id>] [--json] [--propose] reads a goal, says which activities it needs to be visible and which are blind spots, and with --propose files one open decision per goal and function as that function's agent. An agent never decides. The recommendation's home is that open decision, which holds every candidate as an option so the choice stays open and a person can withdraw it (EE-185); no record type is added, because a Discovery venture can write a decision and it/connections starts at Validation and describes a connection the venture already has.
decisions.why: Torian's instruction of 2026-11-26: agents must be hyper-vigilant that tools give the agents and the system visibility over every activity, for example meeting software that records so every meeting has notes, and the venture should favour owning its own tooling. The asymmetry that makes it a rubric is that an agent's work is visible by construction through the router and provenance (EE-031), while a person's work is visible only as far as a tool captures it, so the activities at risk are the ones a person performs or approves and the ones no workflow step writes a record for.

decisions.decision: An agent definition states its goal, not only its ownership, and every rule that binds the definitions together is a check, not prose. Every function workflow carries a goal, the state one run must make true, and measures, the telos measure kinds the run moves, which must be its function's in function.json; a run is done when its done criteria pass, not when its steps have been performed. A trigger's cadence is required for schedule and refused elsewhere, and its route is required for event and refused elsewhere, so no trigger can be written in a shape that is never due. Every agent.md carries six sections in order: What you work toward, What you own, How you work, When you do not know, What you decide, and what you bring up, Skills. What you work toward names the function's purpose and its measures and tells the agent to read foundation/telos and foundation/goals first and to name which goal each run serves. What you own opens with a Writes line whose routes are exactly the write reach functionWrites derives, so the prose an agent reads cannot drift from the rule the router applies. When you do not know says to ask the person what only they can know, else to record the gap as an assumption with what it rests on and what would show it wrong, and never to write a guess as a fact. Every skill a module ships is named by a workflow step or by agent.md, and the skill search walks skills/ at any depth, as the agent spec does. A recommend row's approver is the founder, the chief of staff or the lead whose portfolio holds the function, and agent.md's lead frontmatter is that same lead. A step writes only a route in its function's reach that the router serves with a write action. Every lead role template points its skill at Naive's one generic lead skill, packages/naive/src/interfaces/skills/lead/SKILL.md; a skill per lead is not built. What you own also names how a route is read and written, so no agent has to infer the call from a route name; that paragraph is prose with no derived referent, and it is checked only by check-docs-claims.ts, which fails on a command, flag, path or route the text names and the code lacks. check-functions.ts enforces the rest, and check-functions-test.ts breaks each rule on a copy.
decisions.why: Torian, 2026-11-26: agents need skills and workflows that make clear what we hope to accomplish, agents must know the venture's goals and which of their work serves which goal, and a workflow is walked in order with nothing silently skipped. A review of the 13 function modules (docs/reviews/AGENT_DEFINITIONS_REVIEW_2026-11-26.md) found that 12 of 13 agents never named the telos or the goals, no workflow said what a run was for, none of the 13 said what to do when information is missing, 4 claimed a route the router refuses and 5 omitted routes they hold, and a lead's brief carried a function agent's skill. Prose that nothing checks drifts, so each finding is fixed in the definitions and held by a check.

decisions.decision: Work a venture passed over is kept, and a function agent may spawn a temporary specialist of itself. Skipped work is derived, never a record: `naive skipped` reads the run log and the shipped workflows and lists each occurrence a person skipped and each step the latest finished run that reported its steps left out, in the order APQC's framework gives, with what the item's element feeds downstream when the element graph can tell. A run reports what it finished with `naive due record --steps`, and a run that reports none says nothing about its steps. Nothing judges a step's `when`: it stays a sentence a person or the function's agent reads, so a consider step is listed with its block and is not required. `naive skipped handback` files one open decision asking the owning function agent to recommend do-now, defer or drop, and a person decides; the loop only names how many items wait and never acts on one. A specialist is a record at `operations/specialists/<role>.json` that `naive agent spawn` writes and runs through NAIVE_AGENT_CMD, and its reach is the globs of its record intersected with its parent's own reach, read fresh on every write, so a finished, revoked or expired specialist, or one whose record was widened by hand, is refused before the schema. A spawn needs no person, because the agent is dividing work it may already do and every write still meets the gate as the specialist's own role. The default ttl is an unvalidated prior in `packages/naive/src/engine/specialists.json` that a venture overrides with `specialists.default_ttl` in `naive.config.json`.
decisions.why: Torian decided this on 2026-11-26: work should be walked in hierarchical order with a loop back to what was skipped, and an agent should be able to spawn a temporary specialist for a task its own skills do not cover. Keeping the ledger derived means nothing has to be kept in step with the run log, and intersecting a specialist's globs with its parent's at every write makes a wider reach structurally impossible rather than a rule someone must enforce.

decisions.decision: A public page's words are records before the page exists. Each element a page shows is its own marketing-message record at marketing/message/<id>.json (route marketing/message/[id], function marketing-and-sales, writer function, decision class public-commitment): the tagline, a headline, a subhead, a value proposition, a call to action with its destination, a proof point, an objection answered, the footer and the contact line, each with the words themselves and cites, the records they come from, so a call to action and a contact address finally have a record of their own, destination kind none saying honestly that a button leads nowhere yet. The element catalogue is data, not code: the chrome and the kind of each section's words sit in the marketing matrix's copy block, and the sitemap plans the sections. Need-now suggests the record type from Discovery, so a venture that shows itself to anyone can write its text before it has a brand or a validated solution. naive copy gaps names, element by element, which record holds the words and the state of every record upstream of it, missing, held, undecided or live, the ones only a person writes included, such as foundation/core. naive copy draft --propose files one open decision per missing or undecided element with two or three EE-211 candidates, each a whole record citing its sources and saying which are unsettled, drafted by the marketing and sales agent through the harness in NAIVE_AGENT_CMD, or the prompt is printed and the decision filed with the gap alone. Only a person chooses, and merge writes the record. The order is fixed by the site-copy workflow: gap report, the two paths, options, the founder's choice, the handoff to the builder, then design and the publish check. The copy gate (naive copy check, and stage 0 of the publish build) refuses a build while any element the sitemap plans has no record a person stands behind, and names each one. The founder may skip approval with naive copy one-shot --by <person>, recorded as a decided decision with their name, the time, their reason and the elements skipped, after which every build is marked unapproved; mentura reopen site-copy-one-shot takes it back. No agent ever chooses that path.
decisions.why: Torian decided this on 2026-11-26, building Mentura's own marketing site: he wants the slogan and every other line of a page held as a record, options presented from the records they come from with the specific record named, and his pick asked for before anything is designed, because an agent that writes a page's words has made a public commitment on his behalf. The real run showed the gaps the framework had: foundation/core was empty and only he writes it, foundation/problem was missing, the ICP drafts were stale, and there was no record type for a call to action's label and destination or for a contact address. Brand voice and the validated solution start at Validation, too late for a Discovery page, so what a page needs is routable from Discovery. One-shot exists because it is his venture and his time, and it is named up front with what it costs so the choice is informed, never an agent's.

decisions.decision: Every word a venture publishes passes the publishing gate wherever it is held. The publish lint reads the copy a record holds as well as a page's prose: a marketing sitemap section's draft_copy, and every string under a field the visibility sidecar calls public. A sitemap section takes no field the schema does not name, so copy written into an invented field is refused by name instead of shipping unlinted. A mark is matched case-insensitively and on word boundaries, and a name the venture marks private is an error whatever its rule's severity; severities stay unvalidated priors the venture sets under publish_lint.rules in naive.config.json. The marketing and sales function writes its own marks in marketing/publish-terms.json, which holds names only and never severities or waivers, so the role that owns the words can tighten the gate and never loosen it. Code that reads a venture's config as a file resolves it through configFile in packages/naive/src/core/venture-paths.ts, so a structured venture's meta/naive.config.json is the copy that counts. A decision's unlock still holds an agent's edit of a live record: the lock fails closed, and a stale card is corrected by a person or by deciding. A handoff's inputs are looked for in the venture first, its roles are the one register in packages/naive/src/engine/agents/roles.ts (function agents and researchers included), and the check action of an item route gives a check in ID_CHECKS the item's id.
decisions.why: Torian decided on 2026-11-26 that every word on the site must come from records and pass Naive's publishing gates and lint. A session publishing Mentura's marketing copy through Naive found each of these gaps open: copy in a record was never linted, a private name scored zero errors, a config written through the route was ignored, the role that owns the words could not set its own terms, and a writer-to-builder handoff could not pass its ready check.

decisions.decision: Documents are catalogued as data and built in a fail-closed order. packages/naive/src/functions/documents.json, record type document-catalog, holds the formats (md, pdf, docx, pptx, html, site) with how a person takes each one in and who renders it, the rules for choosing one (a person reading alone and in order takes a document and not slides; a person speaking to a room takes slides, one point a slide; Word only when the reader must edit the words; an interactive page only once the words are settled; public is a one-way door), the ladder, and the document kinds a venture makes: one-pager, memo, brief, meeting-pack, board-update, pitch-deck, spec and site-copy, each naming its function, purpose, audience, artifact kind, the highest rung it climbs, its formats with why those and not the others, and the sections it renders from, each section naming the record it reads. The ladder is one chain, each rung naming the rung it comes after: reading-copy (md, pdf, docx) first, then slides (pptx) or interactive (html), then live (site). A rung is built only once the rung below it exists as a live artifact a person approved, which is the ladder's own requirement, so a rung's requires holds only what it adds; live adds the publication policy and a decided public-commitment decision. requires is written in the shape EE-217's prerequisitesOf reads, records, meetings and decisions, and this decision adds the data and the step order, not the gating mechanism. Approval is a person writing approved_by on the artifact record (artifacts/<kind>-<rung>.json), with document_kind and format added to artifact.schema.json so a check can tell which rung an artifact sits on; there is no new decision class and no new approval mechanism. naive render <kind> writes the Markdown reading copy and its artifact record, every section citing the record and field it came from and every fact no record holds shown as a hole, never written in. Every other format prints what the harness must do instead of rendering, so Naive carries no document dependency; the catalog names no vendor and the harness adapter does, with claude-code.json naming Anthropic's pdf, docx, pptx and xlsx skills (Apache 2.0, adapted and not copied) and artifact-design for a page. check-documents.ts checks the catalog across files and refuses a venture's document that sits on a rung whose rung below is missing or unapproved. The writing-documents skill carries the ladder, the per-format table and the Claude Code section, and marketplace plugins that render through an outside service are skipped because a venture's records would leave the tenant.
decisions.why: Torian decided this on 2026-11-26: before the website gets built, build HTML he can view and interact with, and before that an internal record a human would sit down and read and could print for a meeting. He asked the framework to be opinionated about which documents can be printed and presented, which records become decks and PDFs, when a PowerPoint beats a PDF, which tools make them, and which instructions each agent gets, with Claude Code instructions specifically, and to learn from the plugins that already exist rather than reinvent them. His standing rule decides the shape: a record is the source of truth and a document is a view rendered from records, never the record. The format rules and the word and page counts are unvalidated priors a venture overrides, and only a person approves a rung.
